text.p: The following are the main stories from Tuesday morning's Austrian newspapers:
DER STANDARD
- The restructuring of Vienna's stock exchange should make the bourse more competitive and provide more protection for small shareholders. A new takeover law is expected to be ready before long.
- Former chancellor and Social Democrat party leader Franz Vranitzky looks back without anger on his political career and says politics cannot pretend to be omnipotent.
- Social Democrat general secretary Andreas Rudas defends the decision to choose Tyrol's provincial chief Herbert Prock as one of the new vice party-chiefs instead of Transport Minister Caspar Einem.
- Prices for groceries in Austria are still 12 percent above the European average, says economic research institute WIFO.
DIE PRESSE

- Peter Skaliczky, head of Austria's university principals, criticises the government's decision to continue austerity measures for research and the sciences, saying it could ruin the future of research.
- The constitutional court has decided to change certain passages in the new labour contract laws on the grounds they were not practicable.
- Designated Social Democrat vice party chief Herbert Prock expects the rise of far-right Freedom Party leader Joerg Haider to end by 1999.
- Social Democrats and Conservatives plan to introduce a new passage to the constitution that would grant the right to work.
- The restructuring of Vienna's bourse should lead to a reduction of fees.
- U.S. rating agency Moody's keeps Bank Austria on its watch list after its takeover of Creditanstalt in January, and says Austrian banks' ratings are growing in insecurity.
- Creditanstalt will raise its dividend for 1996 by two schillings to 12 schillings.
- Styria's provincial energy providers are to be brought together into a holding.
- Agricultural income will fall further this year as EU subsidies for Austrian farmers fall to just over two billion schillings in 1997 from seven billion schillings, while prices remain low.
- EU industrial commissioner Martin Bangemann demands that Austria liberalises its telecommunications market as quick as possible and to ensure it will be competitive.
KURIER
- Nazi victims are taking legal action against Austrian insurers and also charge that the state enriched itself when compensation laws ended in 1959.
WIRTSCHAFTSBLATT
- Fibremaker Lenzing will make a profit in 1998 after restructuring measures are completed this year, said chief executive Heinrich Stepnizcka.
